templates.pattern: A resistor has a resistance of [R] Ω and a current of [I] A flowing through it. Calculate the potential difference across the resistor in volts.
templates.explanation:
Using Ohm's Law: V = I × R
= [I] × [R]
= [RESULT] V

Ohm's Law states that the potential difference across a component is directly proportional to the current through it, provided temperature stays constant.

templates.pattern: A potential difference of [V] V is applied across a resistor of [R] Ω. Calculate the current flowing through the resistor in amperes.
templates.explanation:
Using Ohm's Law: I = V ÷ R
= [V] ÷ [R]
= [RESULT] A

Current is measured in amperes (A). A higher resistance means less current flows for the same potential difference.

templates.pattern: A current of [I] A flows through a component when a potential difference of [V] V is applied. Calculate the resistance of the component in ohms.
templates.explanation:
Using Ohm's Law: R = V ÷ I
= [V] ÷ [I]
= [RESULT] Ω

Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω). A component with high resistance requires a large potential difference to drive a small current through it.

templates.pattern: A component has a potential difference of [V] V across it and a current of [I] A flowing through it. Calculate the power dissipated by the component in watts.
templates.explanation:
Electrical Power = Voltage × Current
= P = VI
= [V] × [I]
= [RESULT] W

Power is the rate at which energy is transferred. 1 watt = 1 joule per second.

templates.pattern: A resistor of resistance [R] Ω carries a current of [I] A. Calculate the power dissipated by the resistor in watts.
templates.explanation:
Power = I² × R
= [I]² × [R]
= [I*I] × [R]
= [RESULT] W

This formula is useful when you know the current and resistance but not the voltage. Doubling the current quadruples the power dissipated.

templates.pattern: A potential difference of [V] V is applied across a resistor of [R] Ω. Calculate the power dissipated by the resistor in watts.
templates.explanation:
Power = V² ÷ R
= [V]² ÷ [R]
= [V*V] ÷ [R]
= [RESULT] W

This formula is useful when you know the voltage and resistance but not the current. It is derived by combining P = VI with I = V/R.

templates.pattern: A current of [I] A flows through a [V] V component for [T] seconds. Calculate the electrical energy transferred in joules.
templates.explanation:
Electrical Energy = Voltage × Current × Time
= E = VIt
= [V] × [I] × [T]
= [RESULT] J

This is the total energy transferred to the component. It equals the power multiplied by the time.

templates.pattern: Three resistors of resistance [R1] Ω, [R2] Ω and [R3] Ω are connected in series. Calculate the total resistance of the circuit in ohms.
templates.explanation:
Series resistance: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃
= [R1] + [R2] + [R3]
= [RESULT] Ω

In a series circuit the total resistance is simply the sum of all individual resistances. The same current flows through each component.

templates.pattern: A charge of [Q] C flows past a point in a circuit in [T] seconds. Calculate the current at that point in amperes.
templates.explanation:
Current = Charge ÷ Time
= I = Q ÷ t
= [Q] ÷ [T]
= [RESULT] A

Current is the rate of flow of charge. One ampere means one coulomb of charge passes per second.

templates.pattern: A household uses [KWH] kWh of electricity. The cost of electricity is [PRICE] pence per kWh. Calculate the total electricity bill in pence.
templates.explanation:
Total cost = energy used × cost per unit
= [KWH] × [PRICE]
= [RESULT] pence

To convert to pounds divide by 100. Electricity companies charge per kilowatt-hour. Reducing energy consumption directly reduces the electricity bill.
